To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

DIC microscopy can be used to obtain reliable measurements of the mass of small biological objects, and that this technique is not applicable for the measurement of non‐circular biological objects, unless the orientation of these objects can be determined with high precision.

DIC microscopy can be used to determine the integrated optical path of an object with a precision of about 1–2%, provided the object has a circular shape and is orientated perpendicular to the lateral shift direction.

(i) the integrated optical path length can be reconstructed from DIC images with a precision that is comparable to that of conventional phase contrast microscopy; (ii) the orientation angle of non‐circular test objects influences the measured values, but the artefact can be limited by adjusting the parameters used in the reconstruction procedure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a new technique that allows the determination of mass of biological objects.
the development and evaluation of methods for quantitative optical microscopy.
the application of DIC microscopy for the determination of dry mass.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the method is applicable to circular objects of a certain size and shape, but that for non‐circular or elongated objects the results may be strongly dependent on the orientation of the object.
the DIC technique is suitable for measuring integrated optical pathlengths of biological objects, but that the method is limited by systematic errors.

the technique of reconstructing OPDs from DIC images is very useful for the determination of the dry mass of objects, provided the objects are small, have a circular shape and are orientated parallel to one of the two lateral shifts.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the DIC method for mass determination can be applied successfully for circular objects, and for non‐circular ones provided that they are well orientated with respect to the lateral shift.
the DIC method can be used to measure the dry mass of biological objects, but the method requires careful calibration and optimization for each specific application.

the method of OPD reconstruction from DIC images is a very powerful technique to determine the dry mass of small objects, but that the results obtained for non‐circular shapes are not yet fully reliable.
The main takeaway from our work is that
DIC microscopy is a viable method for measuring the mass of biological specimens.

the method can be used to obtain reliable results on circular objects, but that the method is not yet ready to measure non‐circular or elongated objects, as the results are strongly influenced by the orientation of the objects.
the integrated OPD can be used for mass determination, but that care should be taken in choosing the parameters of the reconstruction procedure.
